properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31. Both earlier states are preserved: the original four-way fork at `snap:epoch:arrival-delta:dec:where-content-lives`, the object_store amendment at `…:r2`.

THREE PARTS, all his word:

1. ADOPT `object_store` (Apache Arrow, originally InfluxData), LOCAL FILESYSTEM ONLY. The `fs` backend is a default feature and `InMemory` needs no feature at all; `aws`/`azure`/`gcp` stay OFF, which keeps `reqwest` and the crypto providers out of the tree. Cloud backends remain one configuration change away with no rework, because the whole point of the crate is that the backend is a runtime detail — so this is the smallest useful slice rather than a narrowing.

2. BLOBS ARE COMMITTED TO THE REPO. Chosen because it is the only option where the bytes are DISTRIBUTED BY THE SAME MECHANISM AS THE DESIGN: clone and you have everything, nothing to configure, nothing to be down, nothing to fall out of step. Every alternative is a second distribution channel, and a second channel is a second thing someone can skip — after which they see a design with holes in it and cannot tell. That is the failure `req:content-reaches-every-seat` exists to prevent. ACCEPTED COSTS, named rather than glossed: repo weight, and git handles binary churn poorly. Text — markdown, mermaid, HTML — diffs and compresses well and is most of what this will hold; raster images are the real risk and are the thing to watch first.

3. THE STORE LIVES IN `reflow2-mcp`, THE POINTER IN `reflow2-core`. Forced by a property worth keeping rather than chosen for taste: `object_store` is async and `fs` pulls tokio, while `reflow2-core` is deliberately synchronous — measured 2026-07-31, its entire dependency list is dynograph-{core,storage,graph,resolution,vector}, serde, serde_json, sha2, with no tokio, no async, no futures. So the core holds the CONTENT HASH, which is sync, deterministic and in-memory-testable, and `reflow2-mcp` does the I/O with the tokio it already carries through rmcp and hyper. Same split as `coverage_report`: the core computes, the surface touches the world.

WHAT MUST HOLD, unchanged by the answers: the pointer is a CONTENT HASH and never a path (`cap:session-memory` already recorded what a path costs — it "resolves for one person on one machine and silently misses for everyone on a shared graph"), and an unresolvable pointer FAILS LOUD and names itself (`req:no-silent-fallback`). Content addressing also keeps this reversible: because a blob can be verified wherever it came from, moving to a different distribution mechanism later changes how bytes are fetched and nothing about what the graph says.

STILL TO CHECK AT BUILD TIME, not decided away: `object_store`'s MSRV against the workspace's 1.94, and its transitive tree with cloud features off MEASURED rather than assumed. Per `dec:design-dependencies-declared` the dependency is DECLARED with its version and the features taken by name — a new crate in this tree is a recorded reliance, not a line in a Cargo.toml.

AND ONE THING DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN: what bounds repo growth. A size cap that refuses oversized blobs loudly was offered and not taken, so nothing currently stops a large binary landing in the history where it cannot be removed without rewriting it. That is the first thing to revisit if the repo starts to hurt, and it is cheaper to add before there is history than after.
properties.name: Content lives in a content-addressed store behind object_store, local backend, COMMITTED to the repo
properties.rationale:
Settled in one pass because Anthony's research had already dissolved the hard part: once `object_store` makes the backend runtime configuration, "which storage" stops being an architectural commitment and only the git question remains — and that one turned out not to be about repo weight at all, but about whether the bytes travel the way the design already travels.

The placement was not a preference. It came from measuring `reflow2-core`'s dependency list and finding it genuinely free of async, which makes "put the store in the core" a decision to spend a property the crate has kept deliberately for a convenience it does not need. Reading the manifest answered in a minute what an argument about layering would not have settled at all.

The open item on repo growth is recorded rather than decided because the honest answer depends on evidence nobody has yet: what actually gets stored. A cap chosen now would be a number invented to feel safe — the asserting default `req:defaults-do-not-assert` exists to prevent — while a cap chosen after a month of real blobs would be measured. The cost of waiting is that git history is unforgiving, and that is exactly why it is named here rather than left to be discovered.
